note: Modes are compatible and stack. Each mode adds mandatory directives and forces a specific deck to be drawn. Stacking more than three modes tends to produce noise rather than strangeness - the draw script warns above three.

modes.label: Infant mode - unlearn function, name, and causality
directives: Ignore the official function of every object involved; treat what it does when misused as what it is for.
Let similar-sounding names imply real kinship between unrelated things, and follow that kinship seriously.
Invert the order of cause and effect at least once and keep the inversion consistent.
Do not maintain the boundaries alive/dead, inside/outside, self/other, real/imagined unless the world's own new law restores them.
Ask 'why must it be so?' of every premise that no one usually states.
modes.guard: Infant logic, adult execution. Childlike results (cute, silly, whimsical for its own sake) are a failure of this mode, not an expression of it.
modes.suits: Origins, first contact, anything whose function should not be assumed: a creature, a rite whose reason was forgotten, a world before naming. Also good when the brief is stale because everyone already agrees what the thing is for.
modes.destroys: Anything with a specification. A tool, a workflow, a game mechanic that must resolve, a service someone pays for: this mode discards learned function, so it discards the requirement with it. The result reads as whimsy, which this mode's own guard calls a failure.

modes.label: Non-anthropocentric mode - remove human usefulness
directives: Nothing here exists for human benefit, and nothing was designed with a human in mind.
Humans, if present, are weather, terrain, or an accident - never the audience.
If the result would be a product, a tool, or a service, it is disqualified in this mode.
Do not give it a humanoid body plan, a face, or motives that map onto human wants.
modes.guard: Check every sentence containing 'so that' or 'in order to'. If the beneficiary is a person, rewrite.
modes.suits: A creature, a world rule, a form of life, a process - subjects where nobody has to want the result. It is the strongest mode in the deck at what it does, and it produced the most genuinely unfamiliar material in every test.
modes.destroys: Any brief with a person in it. It dissolves the asker out of the answer by construction: asked for a ritual a community performs, it returns a process observed by nobody; asked for a two-player game mechanic, it returns something with no players. If the brief names a user, an audience, a player, a reader, a congregation, a customer or a patient, this mode will remove them and the result will not answer the question. This is design guidance, not a measurement: no experiment has isolated this mode's effect, and the fit collapse once attributed to it survived its removal from the default. Choose it on purpose, not by default.

modes.label: Rule-break mode - change physics, time, or selfhood rather than appearance
directives: Delete or invert at least one law of the drawn constraint deck and never restore it quietly.
Install a replacement law that makes something newly impossible; state that impossibility explicitly.
Derive at least three consequences from the new law that you did not intend when you wrote it.
The visual appearance may be perfectly mundane. The strangeness lives in what is possible, not in what is seen.
modes.guard: If deleting the visual description leaves the idea intact, the mode was applied. If it leaves nothing, it was not.
modes.suits: Almost everything. It changes what is possible rather than what is visible, which leaves the brief's subject and its audience intact - a mechanic still resolves, a ritual is still performed by people, a creature still lives somewhere. This is the default for that reason.
modes.destroys: Nothing outright. It is weakest where the brief is about a feeling or a relationship rather than a rule, because there may be no law to break; pair it with affect there.

modes.label: Sense and feeling mode - invent a perception or an unnamed emotion
directives: Invent at least one sense or one affect that has no existing name, and answer all four required fields for it.
Show one ordinary daily situation reorganized by it - a greeting, a queue, a meal, a goodbye.
Name the new injustice, misunderstanding, or grief it creates.
Do not translate the new sense into sight or sound as a shortcut, and do not render feelings as colors.
modes.guard: A sense that only adds convenience is a feature. A sense that adds a new way to be wronged is an invention.
modes.suits: Interior states, senses, relationships, grief, etiquette, anything whose subject is what it is like rather than how it works. Strongest on rituals and on briefs where the interesting part is the misunderstanding.
modes.destroys: Nothing, but it is expensive: it requires an invented sense with all four fields answered, which is a large amount of the result spent on one card. On a brief that is really about a mechanism it crowds out the mechanism.

modes.label: Extremal mode - discard everything safe
directives: Discard every candidate that any competent writer would reach within one minute of hearing the prompt.
Draw twice as many domains and two rules to break instead of one, and hybridize from the three most distant survivors.
Cull harder rather than scoring higher: this mode changes the hand and the discard bar, not the gate.
If nothing survives, report that honestly and show the closest failure with the reason it failed.
modes.guard: Extremal is not louder. It is a stricter cull with the same coherence requirement.
modes.suits: The third attempt, after two rounds the user has already rejected. It widens the hand and doubles the rules to break, so there is more distance to work with.
modes.destroys: A first attempt, usually. Reaching for it early spends the widest material in the deck before the ordinary hand has been tried, and there is nothing wider to escalate to afterwards.

modes.label: Grounded mode - keep the alien principle, add one operational path
directives: Keep the broken law and the new law intact. Do not soften the premise to make it buildable.
Add exactly one section describing how a person could actually encounter, use, or make a version of this within current constraints.
State plainly which part of the principle does not survive that translation.
Never let the operational path retro-edit the principle into something ordinary.
modes.guard: Use with anchor 2 or 3 when the user needs the result for a real product, story, or brief.
modes.note: Scores translation_integrity in place of non_anthropocentrism and requires the operational_path section. It cannot be stacked with nonhuman: the axis it removes is the one nonhuman mode exists to enforce, and score_gate.py refuses the combination.
modes.suits: Anything that has to exist afterwards: a product, a prototype, a shootable scene, a mechanic a group will actually play, a rite a family will actually perform. Use with anchor 2 or 3.
modes.destroys: Nothing, but it is not a rescue. It cannot be stacked with nonhuman, and reaching for it mid-run re-seeds the deal and throws away the hand and everything written against it, so choose it at stage 3 rather than at stage 8.

anchors.label: Unbound
anchors.rule: No requirement of buildability, usefulness, or human relevance. Internal consistency is the only obligation.

anchors.label: Legible
anchors.rule: Must be describable to a non-expert in three sentences without analogy to a known work.

anchors.label: Stageable
anchors.rule: Must be renderable as a concrete scene, artifact, or scenario a team could produce or film.

anchors.label: Operable
anchors.rule: Must include one path to a real prototype, publication, or product, with the loss from that translation stated.

default_modes_note: alien-physics alone. The documented default used to be nonhuman,alien-physics, and this note used to say a controlled experiment had measured what nonhuman cost. That causal attribution is withdrawn. A second, pre-registered experiment ran alien-physics alone on the current build with the self-scored gate threshold removed, and the engine still lost to a plain-prompt control on every brief and every measure: WANT -2.83, FIT -3.03, CRAFT -1.67 as engine minus control, median over five blind judges on 1-7 scales over six briefs, with the control above the engine in 30 of 30 brief x judge cells and holding 90 of 90 top-three slots. Pooled FIT moved only 3.27 -> 3.33 when nonhuman left the default, against a control at 6.35, so the fit collapse was not caused by nonhuman. Convergence was not measurably reduced (g_CORE +0.10, g_SKELETON -0.22 against a required +0.30) and coder reliability of 0.786 and 0.673 fell below the pre-registered .80 floor, making that measure inconclusive rather than favourable. The engine cost 48x the control per output. The pre-registered rule returns FAIL and makes the plain-prompt control the recommended default. nonhuman is still here; its suits/destroys entry is design guidance, not a measured effect. SKILL.md carries the full result.
